## Overview

- Pancreatic adenocarcinoma is one of the **most lethal malignancies**
- Ranks 8th among cancer types in women, 10th in men
- **3rd leading cause** of cancer death in the United States
- Expected to become **2nd most common** cause of cancer death in coming decade
- Lethality reflects:
  - Intrinsic biologic aggressiveness
  - Most patients diagnosed at relatively advanced stage

## Epidemiology & Prognosis

- Over **half** of patients have systemic metastases at diagnosis
- Another **third** have locally advanced disease precluding immediate surgery
- Only **15%–20%** initially present with surgically operable disease
- Surgical resection is the **only** treatment modality associated with long-term survival
- Targeted therapy and immunotherapy have had **limited benefit** thus far
- Risk approximately **doubles** for each decade of life between age 50 and 90

## Clinical Presentation – Early Detection Challenges

- Pancreas cancer is **rarely diagnosed "early"**
- Often relatively **asymptomatic** in initial stages
- Most signs and symptoms are **nonspecific** and **subacute**
- Exception: **jaundice** (more specific)
- Contributes to rarity of early-stage diagnosis

## Clinical Presentation – Symptoms

- **"Painless jaundice"** – classic presentation (head tumors obstructing bile duct)
- Most operable tumors occur in the **pancreatic head**
- Many tumors do **not** obstruct the bile duct
- Most pancreas cancers are **not painless** by diagnosis
- Nonlocalized upper abdominal discomfort present for weeks/months
- Pain radiating to the back = **particularly ominous** (retroperitoneal nerve involvement)
- Pain often **worse at night** when supine, relieved with sitting

## Clinical Presentation – Signs & Symptoms

| Sign/Symptom | Clinical Significance |
|---|---|
| Weight loss | Common, nonspecific |
| Nausea/vomiting | Gastric outlet obstruction |
| Palpable mass | Advanced disease |
| Courvoisier's sign | Gallbladder distension |
| Trousseau's sign | Peripheral venous thrombosis |
| Pancreatitis | Without gallstones/alcohol |
| Pancreatic insufficiency | Exocrine and/or endocrine |

## New-Onset Diabetes & Pancreatic Cancer

- New-onset **insulin-dependent diabetes** after age 60
- Associated with **1%–2% incidence** of previously undiagnosed pancreas cancer
- Important clinical clue for early detection
- Should prompt further evaluation in appropriate clinical context

## Diagnosis – Laboratory Tests

- Initial evaluation with serum blood tests
- **Obstructive jaundice pattern:**
  - Markedly elevated bilirubin
  - Elevated alkaline phosphatase
  - Some elevation of ALT and AST

## CA 19-9 Tumor Marker

- Often **elevated** in pancreas cancer
- **Limitations:**
  - Markedly elevated in benign biliary obstruction
  - ~15%–20% of patients **cannot synthesize** CA 19-9 (Lewis blood group)
  - Limited diagnostic value, especially in jaundiced patients
- **Primary utility:**
  - Following treatment response in nonjaundiced patients
  - Reduction associated with improved survival
  - Negative prognostic factor if markedly elevated

## Other Serum Markers

- **CEA:** Too insensitive/nonspecific for initial diagnosis
- **Emerging approaches (experimental):**
  - Circulating cancer cells
  - Circulating tumor DNA
  - Combined with CA 19-9 and other markers
  - May offer sensitive/specific early diagnosis approach

## Imaging Studies – CT Scanning

- **High-resolution triple-phase contrast-enhanced CT** = primary imaging tool
- Pancreatic carcinomas appear:
  - **Hypoenhancing** on arterial phase
  - **Hypointense/isointense** on venous phase
- CT can define:
  - Regional adenopathy
  - Extrapancreatic extension
  - Vascular involvement
  - Liver/peritoneal metastases

## Imaging Studies – MRI

- **Similar utility** to CT for pancreatic mass assessment
- **May be more useful** for:
  - Defining small liver metastases
  - Characterizing small/indeterminate lesions
  - Assessing **cystic lesions** of the pancreas
  - Long-term follow-up (no radiation exposure)
- Preferred over CT in patients with:
  - Limited renal function
  - Contrast allergy

## Imaging Studies – PET Scanning

- FDG-PET has **limited utility**
- **10%–30%** of pancreas cancers fail to take up FDG tracer (PET negative)
- Benign inflammation may be **erroneously PET positive**
- Greatest utility: defining small indeterminate lesions when:
  - Cannot be well characterized by CT/MRI
  - Low suspicion for benign inflammatory process
- Alternative tracers (e.g., 68-gallium dotatate) for neuroendocrine tumors

## Diagnostic Biopsy – Key Principles

- Definitive diagnosis requires **histopathology**
- **NOT all operable masses require preoperative biopsy**
- Biopsy may be unnecessary if:
  - Radiographic characteristics consistent with carcinoma
  - Amenable to surgical resection
  - Low surgical risk
- Biopsy **recommended** for:
  - Higher surgical risk patients
  - Patients requiring neoadjuvant chemotherapy
  - Patients desiring tissue confirmation before surgery

## EUS-Guided Fine Needle Aspiration (FNA)

- **Most common** nonoperative/preoperative biopsy approach
- Vast majority of lesions can be sampled in experienced hands
- **Important limitation:**
  - Pancreas cancers often highly **fibrotic**
  - <10% of cancer area may harbor nests of cancer cells
  - Remainder = fibrous stroma
  - **10%–20% false-negative rate** due to sampling error
- EUS may be **more sensitive** than axial imaging for:
  - Vascular involvement
  - Suspicious peripancreatic lymph nodes

## Alternative Biopsy Approaches

- **ERCP with brushings:**
  - For lesions causing biliary obstruction
  - Inferior sensitivity to EUS-FNA
  - Risk of pancreatitis (can be severe)
  - Rarely performed for diagnosis alone
- **Percutaneous biopsy** (US or CT-guided):
  - Option when EUS-FNA unsuccessful
  - Can target primary tumor or metastases
  - Tumor seeding risk: ~0.1% (very rare)

## ERCP – Role in Management

- **Diagnostic role:** Limited (inferior to EUS-FNA)
- **Therapeutic role:** Biliary stenting for jaundice relief
  - Indicated for inoperable disease
  - Or planned neoadjuvant chemotherapy
- **Stent selection:**
  - **Metallic wall stents** preferred for neoadjuvant candidates
  - Plastic stents require replacement every 2–3 months
- **Routine preoperative stenting NOT supported** by randomized data
- Preoperative biliary intervention associated with **higher postoperative infection rate**

## Diagnostic Laparoscopy

- Purpose: Define/exclude metastatic disease before resection
- Early studies: 20%–30% with "resectable" disease had occult metastases
- With improved CT: yield now **<10%**
- **Selective approach warranted:**
  - Large tumors (T3 or T4)
  - Indeterminate liver lesions on imaging
  - Markedly elevated CA 19-9

## Cancer Staging – AJCC 8th Edition (2016)

- Combines **T** (tumor), **N** (nodes), **M** (metastases)
- Stages I through IV
- **Key changes from prior editions:**
  - T1: <2 cm; T2: 2–4 cm; T3: >4 cm
  - T4: SMA or celiac artery involvement
  - N0: node negative; N1: 1–3 nodes; N2: >3 nodes
  - M1: distant metastasis

## AJCC Staging Table – T Classification

| Stage | T | N | M | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | Tis | N0 | M0 | Carcinoma in situ (PanIN3) |
| IA | T1 | N0 | M0 | Tumor ≤2 cm, limited to pancreas |
| IB | T2 | N0 | M0 | Tumor >2 cm and <4 cm |
| IIA | T3 | N0 | M0 | Tumor >4 cm |
| IIB | T1–T3 | N1 | M0 | 1–3 regional LN metastasis |
| III | T4 | N2 | M0 | SMA/celiac involvement and/or ≥4 LN |
| IV | Any | Any | M1 | Distant metastasis |

## Five-Year Survival by Stage

| Stage | 5-Year Survival |
|---|---|
| IA | ~40% |
| IB | ~30% |
| IIA | ~25% |
| IIB | ~13% |
| III | ~10% |

- Validated using multiple datasets (US, Europe, Asia)
- Stage IIA now more objectively defined (tumor >4 cm)
- Stage III includes N2 nodal involvement with any T stage

## Treatment Overview

- **Surgical resection** = only treatment with long-term survival
- Assessment for resectability = critical initial step
- Multidisciplinary tumor board evaluation recommended
- Experienced pancreatic surgeon at **high-volume center** essential
- Patients categorized as:
  - Resectable
  - Borderline resectable / Locally advanced
  - Metastatic

## Resectable Disease – Criteria

- **No** evidence of metastatic disease
- **No** SMA or celiac artery involvement/abutment
- Portal/SMV involvement:
  - None, OR
  - Venous involvement that can be **readily resected en bloc** for R0 resection

## Figure 62.1 – Resectable Tumor

- Pancreatic adenocarcinoma in head/uncinate process
- **Well-preserved fat plane** (arrow) between tumor (T) and superior mesenteric artery (A)
- Clear separation indicates resectability
- No vascular invasion

## Borderline Resectable Disease

- Tumor **proximity to or direct involvement** of venous/arterial structures
- Venous involvement potentially resectable with reconstruction
- Arterial involvement: **<180 degrees** of SMA or celiac artery circumference
- May be grossly resectable but likely **R1 or R2** margins
- Better termed **"borderline unresectable"**
- Should receive **initial chemotherapy ± radiation** to attempt downstaging

## Locally Unresectable Disease

- More extensive vascular involvement:
  - **Complete encasement** of portal/SMV (not reconstructible)
  - More extensive arterial involvement
- Only potentially resectable with **R2 (grossly positive)** resection
- Low but some potential for response to treatment
- Treatment slows tumor growth, improves survival

## Metastatic Disease

- **Largest subset** of pancreas cancer patients
- Managed with **systemic chemotherapy**
- Surgery/radiation only for **palliation** of specific symptoms
- Systemic therapy has improved in recent years
- Improvements translated to:
  - Adjuvant setting
  - Neoadjuvant treatment for borderline/locally unresectable tumors

## Advances in Chemotherapy – Historical

- Before 1997: Single-agent **5-FU** (unclear survival benefit)
- 1997 (Burris et al.): **Gemcitabine** superior to 5-FU
  - Survival: 5.6 vs 4.4 months
  - Improved quality of life (clinical benefit response)
- Next 16 years: Multiple gemcitabine combinations **failed** to show incremental benefit

## FOLFIRINOX – A Breakthrough (2011)

- Combination: **5-FU + Irinotecan + Oxaliplatin**
- Compared to gemcitabine monotherapy:
  - Median survival: **11 vs 6 months** (nearly doubled)
  - Quality of life improved
  - Partial response: **31% vs 9%**
  - Significant number survived **>12 months**
- More toxic but more effective

## Gemcitabine + Nab-Paclitaxel (2013)

- Von Hoff et al.
- **Gemcitabine + nab-paclitaxel (GA)** vs gemcitabine alone
- Survival: **9 vs 7 months**
- Tumor shrinkage: **23% vs 7%**
- Both FOLFIRINOX and GA superior to single-agent gemcitabine
- FOLFIRINOX may be superior but more toxic

## Surgical Treatment – Resectable Disease

| Location | Procedure |
|---|---|
| Pancreatic head | Pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple) |
| Pancreatic body/tail | Distal pancreatectomy ± splenectomy |
| Extensive intrapancreatic spread | Total pancreatectomy (rare) |

- Marked improvements in **short-term outcomes** (morbidity/mortality)
- Minimally invasive approaches (laparoscopy, DaVinci robot) emerging
- Comparable short-term results with open vs minimally invasive
- Technical modifications have **not** improved long-term oncologic outcomes beyond R0 resection

## Figure 62.2 – Unresectable Tumor

- Pancreatic adenocarcinoma in head/uncinate process
- **Loss of fat plane** (arrow) between tumor (T) and SMA (A)
- Indicates vascular invasion/unresectability
- Metallic endoprosthesis in distal common bile duct (palliative stent)

## Adjuvant Therapy – Historical Progress

| Trial | Treatment | Key Finding |
|---|---|---|
| GITSG | 5-FU + radiation | MS 20 vs 11 months; 2-yr survival 43% |
| CONKO-001 | Gemcitabine vs none | 5-yr survival 21% vs 9% |
| ESPAC-3 | Gemcitabine vs 5-FU/LV | Similar outcomes (~high teens 5-yr) |

## Adjuvant Therapy – Modern Era

| Trial | Treatment | Key Finding |
|---|---|---|
| ESPAC-4 | Gem + Capecitabine vs Gem | 5-yr survival: 29% vs 17% |
| PRODIGE-24 | FOLFIRINOX vs Gemcitabine | MS: **54 vs 35 months** |

- R0 resection + combination therapy → median survival 39 months, 5-yr >40%
- Increasingly effective combinations = improved long-term survival
- FOLFIRINOX more toxic but superior

## Neoadjuvant vs Adjuvant Therapy

**Advantages of Neoadjuvant:**
- Ensures all patients receive chemotherapy
- Biologic test of tumor aggressiveness
- Potential tumor shrinkage → increased R0 resections
- Avoids surgery in patients with early metastatic progression

**Counter-arguments:**
- Tumor progression may lose surgical window
- Low radiologic response rate (~31%)
- Chemotherapy toxicity may delay/abandon surgery

## PREOPANC Trial (Dutch)

- Only published **randomized** neoadjuvant vs adjuvant trial
- Neoadjuvant: Chemoradiation + gemcitabine → surgery → gemcitabine
- Adjuvant: Surgery → gemcitabine
- Included both resectable AND borderline patients
- **Limitations:**
  - Different treatments in each arm
  - Mixed patient population
  - Underpowered
- Result: No overall survival difference (ITT); more benefit in borderline/locally unresectable subgroup

## Borderline Resectable & Locally Unresectable – Neoadjuvant Results

- Neoadjuvant chemotherapy may render lesion resectable:
  - **30%–60%** of borderline resectable
  - Smaller fraction of locally unresectable
- Patients who undergo resection after neoadjuvant: survival **equal** to initially resectable patients
- Role of radiation therapy: **controversial**
  - Alliance trial closed radiation arm early (lack of efficacy)
  - LAP07 trial: no advantage to chemoradiation
- Stereotactic ablative radiation may improve local control

## Post-Treatment Imaging Limitations

- Radiologic assessment after neoadjuvant therapy does **NOT accurately predict resectability**
- Cannot discriminate:
  - Residual cancer adjacent to vessels
  - Residual scar tissue (tumor-free)
- Surgeons need **low threshold** for surgical exploration
- Requires skill to mobilize and safely remove tumors near major arteries

## Formal Arterial Resection – Historical

- 1970s–80s: "Regional pancreatectomy" at MSKCC and NCI
- Arterial + venous resections en bloc with pancreatectomy
- **Extraordinarily high** morbidity and mortality
- **Few long-term survivors**
- Led to view: arterial involvement requiring resection = generally **not appropriate** for surgery

## Appleby Procedure – Exception

- For locally advanced **pancreatic body tumors** involving upper celiac artery
- Requirements:
  - Celiac origin from aorta free of tumor
  - Intact GDA and proper hepatic artery (uninvolved)
  - Ideally aberrant right hepatic artery from SMA
- Resect celiac + common hepatic artery en bloc with distal pancreatectomy
- Depends on **retrograde GDA flow** for hepatic arterial supply
- Major risk: **liver failure**
- "Supercharge" with arterial bypass graft described
- Select patients: survival similar to resectable tumors

## Arterial Resection After Neoadjuvant Therapy

- Some patients with arterial abutment can achieve **R0 margins** post-neoadjuvant
- Selective arterial resection/reconstruction of celiac/SMA
- **Higher risk:** increased morbidity and mortality
- Unclear long-term survival benefit
- Most patients eventually succumb to **metastatic disease** regardless
- Ablative radiation may reduce need for arterial resection
- Should be **highly selective**, performed only by experienced surgeons/centers

## Surgical Palliation

- Unresectable/recurrent cancers cause obstruction:
  - Biliary tree
  - Duodenum
  - Intestine
- Historic "double bypass" (gastrojejunostomy + choledochojejunostomy):
  - Significant morbidity/mortality
  - **Largely supplanted** by nonoperative approaches
- Current management:
  - **Biliary obstruction:** Endoscopic/percutaneous stents
  - **Duodenal obstruction:** Endoluminal stents
  - Surgical palliation (gastrojejunostomy): now **infrequent**

## Advances in Cancer Biology – Diagnosis

- **Circulating tumor DNA:**
  - Predicts recurrence **months ahead** of imaging
  - May aid early identification in high-risk populations
- **Radiomic analysis:**
  - Potential to define tumor prognosis from imaging
- **Combined biomarker approaches:**
  - ctDNA + protein markers
  - May enable earlier detection

## Advances in Cancer Biology – Genomics & Treatment

- **Genomic characterization:**
  - Distinct subsets with markedly different prognoses
  - Some subtypes may benefit from specific chemotherapy
  - May guide FOLFIRINOX vs GA selection
- **KRAS targeting:**
  - Drug targeting of mutant K-ras oncogene demonstrated
  - Common molecular driver of pancreas cancer
- **Immunotherapy:**
  - Mismatch repair deficiency (Lynch syndrome) → response to checkpoint inhibitors
  - Suggests potential for immune stimulation in standard pancreatic cancer

## Key Takeaways

1. Pancreatic cancer remains highly lethal; early diagnosis is rare
2. **Surgical resection** is the only path to long-term survival
3. Multidisciplinary approach at **high-volume centers** is essential
4. CA 19-9 has limited diagnostic value but useful for monitoring
5. Triple-phase CT is the primary imaging modality
6. EUS-FNA is the preferred biopsy method (10–20% false-negative rate)
7. FOLFIRINOX and GA have transformed systemic therapy
8. Neoadjuvant therapy is increasingly important for borderline/locally advanced disease
9. R0 resection remains the surgical goal
10. Emerging biology (ctDNA, genomics, KRAS targeting, immunotherapy) offers future hope

## Summary – Treatment Algorithm

```
Suspected Pancreatic Cancer
        │
        ▼
  Imaging (CT/MRI)
        │
        ▼
  Staging & Assessment
        │
   ┌────┼────────────┐
   ▼    ▼            ▼
Resectable  Borderline/LA  Metastatic
   │         │              │
   ▼         ▼              ▼
Surgery   Neoadjuvant    Systemic
   │      ± Radiation    Chemo
   ▼         │
Adjuvant  Reassess
Chemo     for Surgery
```

## Future Directions

- **Earlier diagnosis:** Liquid biopsies (ctDNA, circulating tumor cells)
- **Personalized therapy:** Genomic subtyping to guide chemotherapy selection
- **KRAS-targeted therapy:** Direct targeting of most common driver mutation
- **Immunotherapy:** Expanding beyond Lynch syndrome patients
- **Improved radiation:** Stereotactic ablative approaches
- **Better surgical selection:** Biomarkers and imaging to predict resectability
- **Clinical trials:** Enrollment should be encouraged
